newsitem.title: USA: USTR Barshefsky says Japan "stalled" on auto accord.
newsitem.headline: USTR Barshefsky says Japan "stalled" on auto accord.

text.p: U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Monday that the U.S. automotive trade deficit with Japan is getting worse and that Tokyo has fallen short in fulfilling an agreement to open its market.

"There is no question that Japan has stalled on deregulation in this sector. That is of significant concern and inexcusable," Barshefsky said in an interview with Reuters. "There is no question that the number of vehicle dealerships is also not adequate."

A 1995 U.S.- Japan trade agreement, reached after contentious negotiations in which the two countries neared the brink of a trade war, calls on Tokyo to deregulate automotive parts markets in order to give foreign suppliers more access. It also calls on the Japanese government to encourage more dealers to sell American brand cars.

Since the agreement, the trade deficit in the automotive sector has deteriorated, not improved, according to Barshefsky. She said the automotive sector now accounts for 66 percent of the U.S. deficit with Japan, compared to 60 percent two years ago.

"The numbers are disturbing," said Barshefsky, who along with U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has told Tokyo that Washington does not want Japan to run up significant surpluses or export its way out of economic difficulties.
The number of Japanese automobile dealers that have signed up to sell cars made by Chrysler Corp., Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Co. has fallen far short of expectations.

The American Automobile Manufacturers Association said that since the 1995 agreement was signed, 126 new dealerships have agreed to sell American cars. That is far short of the 200 expected by the end of the first year of the agreement and the 400 that were expected by the end of 1997.
Barshefsky said the United States will raise those issues during a review of the auto trade accord in September.
That is one of a number of issues that could heighten U.S. trade tensions with Japan over the next few months.

An agreement with Japan on procurement of telecommunications equipment by Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp. (NTT) is set to expire in September and the two sides will sit down for talks next week.

The United States has said it expected American companies to gain a bigger share of equipment sales to NTT and its subsidiaries give the competitiveness of U.S. firms in other markets and in sales to the private sector in Japan.

At the same time, U.S. officials are gearing up for more talks with Japan on civil aviation. Washington has been pushing for an "open skies" agreement that would remove limits on service, but Tokyo is resisting that idea.

The United States and Japan will also be trying to resolve a dispute over Japanese port practices. The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission has suspended proposed sanctions against Japanese shipping companies until Sept. 4 to give Japan time to resolve some of the port issues that Washington says are unfair to foreign liners.

On China, Barshefsky said talks were being held in Geneva this week on Beijing's bid to join the World Trade Organisation. Bilateral talks between the United States and China will take place later this week. But Barshefsky said that, based on what U.S. officials heard of talks with other WTO partners this week, Beijing's latest offer was "tepid."
She said Beijing has been "unresponsive" to concerns of some countries, particularly the European Union.
"We will see what they do in our bilateral," she added.
